{{nihongo|'''Tihiro Ohkawa'''|大河千弘|Ōkawa Chihiro|January 3, 1928 - September 27, 2014|lead=yes}}<ref name="Nihon University - 平成21 - 大河千 弘と核融合研究">{{cite web|url=https://www.cst.nihon-u.ac.jp/research/gakujutu/53/pdf/O-30.pdf |script-title=ja:大河千弘と核融合研究|last=Amemiya|first=Takahisa|date=2009|publisher=[[Nihon University]]|language=ja|access-date=8 September 2018}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aip.org/history-programs/niels-bohr-library/oral-histories/35130|title=Tihiro Ohkawa|date=2015-03-16|website=www.aip.org|language=en|access-date=2020-02-25}}</ref> was a Japanese [[physicist]] whose field of work was in [[Plasma (physics)|plasma physics]] and [[fusion power]]. He was a pioneer in developing ways to generate electricity by [[nuclear fusion]] when he worked at [[General Atomics]].<ref name="SanDiego">{{Cite news|url=http://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/news/science/sdut-physics-generalatomics-ohkawa-2014oct07-story.html|title=Renowned physicist Ohkawa dies at 86|last=Robbins|first=Gary|work=[[The San Diego Union-Tribune]]|access-date=2018-09-08|language=en-US}}</ref> Ohkawa died September 27, 2014, in [[La Jolla, California]], at the age of 86.<ref name="SanDiego" />

== Early life and career ==
Ohkawa was born in [[Kanazawa]] on January 3, 1928.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Maisel|first=Merry|date=2014-10-29|title=Tihiro Ohkawa|journal=[[Physics Today]]|issue=10 |page=10414 |language=EN|doi=10.1063/pt.5.6106|bibcode=2014PhT..2014j0414M }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E5%A4%A7%E6%B2%B3%E5%8D%83%E5%BC%98-1059850|title=大河千弘(おおかわ ちひろ)とは|last=日本人名大辞典+Plus|first=デジタル版|website=コトバンク|language=ja|access-date=2020-02-24}}</ref> He studied physics at the [[University of Tokyo]] in 1950, and was a member of the [[Yoshio Nishina]] group for researching cosmic altitude radiation for 16 years even during the [[World War II]].<ref name=":0"/> He was a researcher at [[CERN]] and at [[Midwestern State University]] before becoming a professor at the [[University of Tokyo]]. In 1960, he went to [[General Atomics]], where he led a fusion research project and later became vice president and deputy chairman of the board.

In 1994, Ohkawa left General Atomics to found TOYO Technologies. In 2004, he was co-founder of Nano Fusion Technologies with Masano Nishikawa for the development of [[microfluidics]]. He was also a physics professor at the [[University of California, San Diego]].

== Scientific contributions ==
In 1955, Ohkawa independently came up with idea of the [[fixed-field alternating gradient accelerator]] (FFAG) together with [[Keith Symon]] and [[Andrei Kolomensky]], which led to the development of the first prototype in 1956 by the [[Midwestern Universities Research Association]] (MURA). He then developed a procedure to stabilize instabilities in [[tokamak]]s using [[Multipole magnet|multipole magnetic fields]] with [[Donald William Kerst|Donald Kerst]] in 1960,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ohkawa|first1=T.|last2=Kerst|first2=D. W.|date=1961|title=Stable Plasma Confinement by Multipole Fields|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=7|issue=2|pages=41–42|doi=10.1103/physrevlett.7.41|bibcode=1961PhRvL...7...41O|issn=0031-9007}}</ref> which was then later confirmed by experiments.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ohkawa|first1=T.|last2=Yoshikawa|first2=M.|last3=Kribel|first3=R. E.|last4=Schupp|first4=A. A.|last5=Jensen|first5=T. H.|date=1970|title=Plasma Confinement in dc Octopole|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=24|issue=3|pages=95–98|doi=10.1103/physrevlett.24.95|bibcode=1970PhRvL..24...95O|issn=0031-9007}}</ref>

In 1968, Ohkawa demonstrated that the plasma-current multipole configuration used to trap plasmas was stable,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ohkawa|first1=T.|last2=Voorhies|first2=H. G.|date=1969|title=Plasma-Current Multipole Experiments|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=22|issue=24|pages=1275–1277|doi=10.1103/physrevlett.22.1275|bibcode=1969PhRvL..22.1275O|issn=0031-9007}}</ref> which resulted in the development of a series of tokamaks with vertically elongated plasma cross sections called the ''doublet''.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Meade|first=Dale|date=2009|title=50 years of fusion research|journal=Nuclear Fusion|volume=50|issue=1|article-number=014004|doi=10.1088/0029-5515/50/1/014004|s2cid=17802364 |issn=0029-5515}}</ref> This eventually led to General Atomics' [[DIII-D (tokamak)|DIII-D tokamak]], which influenced the design and concept of [[ITER]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://fusion.gat.com/global/diii-d/home?redirect=1|title=diii-d:home [MFE: DIII-D and Theory]|website=fusion.gat.com|access-date=2020-02-24}}</ref>

Ohkawa was also involved in the use of [[radioactive isotopes]] in the separation of nuclear isotopes from nuclear waste (at the Archimedes Technology Group in San Diego, which he founded).<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Cluggish|first1=B.P.|last2=Ohkawa|first2=T.|last3=Agnew|first3=S.F.|last4=Freeman|first4=R.L.|last5=Miller|first5=R.L.|last6=Putvinski|first6=S.|last7=Sevier|first7=L.|last8=Umstadter|first8=K.R.|title=IEEE Conference Record - Abstracts. PPPS-2001 Pulsed Power Plasma Science 2001. 28th IEEE International Conference on Plasma Science and 13th IEEE International Pulsed Power Conference (Cat. No.01CH37255) |chapter=Separation of radionuclides from nuclear waste by a plasma mass filter |page=323|publisher=IEEE|doi=10.1109/ppps.2001.961000|isbn=0-7803-7141-0|year=2001}}</ref>

Ohkawa holds over 50 patents, in areas such as tile accelerators, [[fusion technology]] and [[biotechnology]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://aries.ucsd.edu/FPA/ARC98/fpn98-16.shtml|title=FPA Program Notes|website=aries.ucsd.edu|access-date=2020-02-24|archive-date=2016-03-04|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304214405/http://aries.ucsd.edu/FPA/ARC98/fpn98-16.shtml}}</ref>

== Honors and awards ==
In 1968, Ohkawa became a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=1968&unit_id=DPP&institution=|title=APS Fellow Archive|website=www.aps.org|language=en|access-date=2020-02-24}}</ref> In 1979, he received the [[James Clerk Maxwell Prize for Plasma Physics]] for "''his development of multi-current or doublet approach to the design of tokamaks with non-circular cross sections and for investigation of plasma confinement in toroidal multipoles''".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Ohkawa&first_nm=Tihiro&year=1979|title=1979 James Clerk Maxwell Prize for Plasma Physics Recipient|website=American Physical Society|language=en|access-date=2020-02-24}}</ref>

He also received the 1984 Fusion Power Associates Leadership Award.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://fusionpower.org/Awards.html|title=FPA Awards|website=fusionpower.org|access-date=2020-02-24}}</ref>
